title: A Worked Example of How I Redesign AI-Vulnerable Assessments
author: Matthews, Paul
summary: Paul Matthews, a department head at an independent Australian school, walks through how he redesigned a Year 10 history essay task to survive the AI era, using it as a worked example of a broader assessment-redesign method. His approach layers several deliberate moves: anchoring the task explicitly to the department's formation-goal vision (not just a grade), setting a specific AI-use tier on his 'AI Assessment Scale' that permits research but bans AI composition, providing scaffolding so struggling students aren't tempted to outsource out of desperation, adding checkpoint due dates to increase visibility into student progress, and closing with short tactical feedback plus a 'celebration and commission' ritual. The piece's real argument, stated explicitly near the end, is that most of these moves aren't AI-specific at all — they're simply good teaching practice that AI has made newly urgent rather than newly necessary.
points: Treat 'the burden of proof' as reversed: assume students will use AI unless a task and its rules are explicitly designed otherwise.
A tiered AI-use scale (e.g., allowed for research, banned for composition) gives students and teachers a shared, checkable standard instead of vague honor-code language.
Scaffolding (sentence starters, worked examples) reduces AI misuse driven by a task feeling out of reach, not just misuse driven by laziness.
Multiple checkpoint due dates convert a single high-stakes deadline into early-warning visibility that catches drift before it becomes outsourcing.
Feedback works best pared down to one praise and one specific, adoptable fix — not exhaustive commentary most students won't act on.
quotes: Students have had access to AI for their entire high school life. If we say nothing about AI we might assume that they won't use it, but it's likely that the burden of proof runs the other direction for our students.
We decided to make this a level 2 task, meaning AI could be used for finding sources and gathering data, but it could not be used for writing composition.
As I argued last week, one of the reasons students misuse AI is that they feel the task is beyond them. In order to support those who need it, we provided scaffolding for writing composition.

Another risk factor for AI misuse is a lack of visibility. Students can delay work, get to the last minute, panic, then outsource their task. To combat this, we set multiple checkpoints along the way.

I encourage my team to give one point of praise highlighting something that was done really well, and one specific fix that should be adopted in all future work. We've found this kind of feedback is the most actionable for the most students.

And that highlights a core truth about education in an AI world: while we need to make some changes, good teaching remains good teaching. AI has changed a number of things about education, but it's not as if we need to burn it all down and rebuild from the ashes.
